growth_story.headline: Viet Nam's income per person has grown 5.3 percent a year since 1990, with no lasting slowdown through inflation bouts, COVID and a property slump.
growth_story.arc: The data show one long era: income per person grew 5.3 percent a year from 1990 to 2025, with no lasting shift up or down. The World Bank traces this run to the market reforms of Doi Moi, begun in 1986, which moved Viet Nam away from a planned economy. Growth reached 7.7 percent in 1995, eased to 3.4 in 1999 and slowed to 3.7 in 2008, a year when prices rose 23.1 percent; the IMF links that bout of inflation, and another in 2011, to capital inflows after joining the WTO and to loose policy after the global financial crisis. The last ten years averaged 5.3 percent, a little faster than the 4.8 of 2006 to 2015, and Viet Nam ranks first of 11 structural peers, whose median was 1.7. COVID cut growth to 1.9 percent in 2020 and 1.7 in 2021, and turmoil in property and finance held it to 4.3 in 2023. Growth then rose to 7.4 in 2025, when income per person reached 4,308 dollars (constant 2015 prices), its highest level yet.

threads.title: Doi Moi and three decades
threads.text: Market reforms from 1986 moved Viet Nam away from a planned economy toward a market economy. The World Bank describes the decades since as a run of steady growth and falling poverty that few countries have matched.

citations.title: Viet Nam 2045: Breaking Through - Institutions for a High-Income Future
citations.quote: The sustained high rate of growth, averaging 5 to 6 percent over three decades, is an achievement that very few countries can match.

citations.title: Viet Nam 2045: Breaking Through - Institutions for a High-Income Future
citations.quote: Viet Nam has achieved much in the decades since Doi Moi—greatly reduced poverty, economic growth that many countries envy, and improved human development outcomes.

threads.title: Inflation bouts in 2008 and 2011
threads.text: Prices rose 23.1 percent in 2008 and 18.7 percent in 2011. The IMF says both bouts began with outside shocks and were made worse by loose policy, the first after capital poured in following WTO entry. Growth of income per person slowed to 3.7 percent in 2008 and 4.3 in 2012, but did not stall.

citations.title: Vietnam: 2012 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 12/165)
citations.quote: Both episodes appear to have originated with external shocks, but were exacerbated by loose macroeconomic policies.

citations.title: Vietnam: 2012 Article IV Consultation (IMF Country Report No. 12/165)
citations.quote: While the 2008 episode was related to large unsterilized capital inflows in the aftermath of WTO accession

threads.title: COVID and the 2021 outbreak
threads.text: Early containment kept growth positive in 2020, at 1.9 percent, but a severe outbreak from April 2021 caused a sharp fall in output, and growth for the year was 1.7. Growth bounced back to 7.7 percent in 2022.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2022 Article IV Consultation with Vietnam

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2022 Article IV Consultation with Vietnam

threads.title: Property, bonds and bank strain
threads.text: Turmoil in the property sector, financial distress and a drop in exports slowed growth of income per person to 4.3 percent in 2023. The World Bank still points to very high company debt and strained bank liquidity in 2026.

citations.title: IMF Executive Board Concludes 2024 Article IV Consultation with Vietnam
citations.quote: Key headwinds in 2023: turbulence in the real estate sector, financial distress, and a significant drop in exports.

citations.title: Viet Nam Economic Update: Sustaining Reforms, Navigating Uncertainty

threads.title: An export model under pressure
threads.text: Exports and foreign investment lifted growth again in 2024. The IMF and the World Bank both describe new strain on this export-led model from shifting trade policy, an ageing population and, since March 2026, an oil shock tied to the Middle East conflict.

since_last_year.text: Income per person grew 7.4 percent in 2025, the fastest since 2022, and reached its highest level yet. The World Bank describes a sweeping reorganisation of the state, with a wave of new laws and decrees, and an oil shock since March 2026 that weighs on the outlook.

citations.quote: Since 2025, the authorities have enacted more than 86 laws and 300 decrees through to April 2026 to streamline bureaucracy

growth_story.tension: The sources describe repeated bouts of instability, with prices rising 23.1 percent in 2008 and 18.7 percent in 2011 and turmoil in property and finance in 2023, yet the data show no lasting break: growth of income per person stayed above 3 percent every year from 1991 to 2019 and averaged 5.3 percent over 1990 to 2025. The sources also describe a growth model under strain, while the last ten years (5.3 percent) were faster than the ten before (4.8).
